new.title: Claim a terrace seat at Café Ledig Erf
new.desc: This café sits on the Tolsteegbrug at the southern tip of the old town, where the Oudegracht meets the singel. It pours more than 80 beers with taps that change often, and its big terrace has been an Utrecht meeting place for years.
new.tip: They do not take reservations, so just walk in. It opens mid afternoon on weekdays and at noon at the weekend; on the terrace you order by QR code.

new.title: Dine at the top of the Rotsoord water tower
new.desc: The 37 metre water tower between Heuveloord and the Vaartsche Rijn was built in 1906 and 1907 and given back its original look in a 1996 restoration. Restaurant De Watertoren now cooks inside it, with local and where possible organic produce and a wide view over the city.
new.tip: Book ahead and ask for a window table around sunset. They also serve lunch, and Café Brutal in the same tower works for a drink without a full dinner.

new.title: Eat Indonesian classics at Indonesia Asli
new.desc: This restaurant on Biltstraat has been serving traditional Indonesian cooking for around four decades. You can sit down in the dining room or do what many neighbours do and take dinner home from the takeaway counter.
new.tip: Biltstraat is the city's street for affordable world food, so it is easy to combine with a walk through Wittevrouwen. Check the opening hours first, as the kitchen closes fairly early.

new.title: Drink Utrecht beer with the locals at Café Lombok
new.desc: On Vleutenseweg in the heart of Lombok, this easygoing neighbourhood café is run by the Utrecht brewery vandeStreek. It serves lunch, bar snacks and dinner alongside Utrecht beers, with no pretence and plenty of regulars.
new.tip: It opens at 15:00 from Monday to Thursday and at noon from Friday to Sunday. Walk here along Kanaalstraat to see the neighbourhood on the way.

new.title: Have breakfast in the farmhouse bakery of Vroeg
new.desc: Vroeg fills a monumental farmhouse from 1599 on the Achterdijk near Bunnik, which served as an inn until 1735. Its bakery turns out fresh bread all day, and the restaurant cooks with ingredients from the region from breakfast through to dinner.
new.tip: Cycle here from the city through Amelisweerd and Rhijnauwen, about half an hour. The bakery shop sells loaves to take home, and weekend mornings are busy so reserve.

new.title: Snack your way round the Vredenburg market
new.desc: The city's main open air market sets up on Vredenburg square, between the station and the old town, on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays. It is where locals do their shopping for fresh food, and a good place to eat as you go.
new.tip: Saturday is the biggest day. Afterwards walk on to the flower market along the Oudegracht and the plant market on Janskerkhof, which are also held on Saturdays.

new.title: Board the old trains at the Spoorwegmuseum
new.desc: The national railway museum has occupied the 1874 Maliebaan station since 1954. Behind the station hall, themed worlds take you from the first steam engines to modern trains, including a dark ride called Stalen Monsters and the early locomotive De Arend on its own stretch of broad gauge track.
new.tip: Allow at least half a day, more with children. It is a pleasant walk from the centre along the Maliebaan, and the museum is normally closed on Mondays.

new.title: Climb the rock garden at the Botanic Gardens
new.desc: Utrecht University's botanic gardens cover 10 hectares around the old Fort Hoofddijk at the Science Park, the largest academic garden in the country with more than 10,000 plant species. The rock garden, the bamboo grove and the evolution garden are among the highlights.
new.tip: Check the opening dates before you go. The tropical greenhouses are being replaced by new ones and are closed during the works, but the outdoor gardens stay open.

new.title: Follow the snaking wall at Slot Zuylen
new.desc: This castle in the village of Oud-Zuilen marks the start of the Vecht country and has a history going back to the 13th century. The writer Belle van Zuylen lived here, and the grounds are edged by a 120 metre serpentine wall built in 1742.
new.tip: Cycle out from Utrecht along the Vecht, about 6 km. The house is visited as a museum, so check the opening days, and keep following the river north for more country houses.

new.title: Stand under the towers of Kasteel Duurstede
new.desc: Two towers remain of the castle of Wijk bij Duurstede: a heavy brick keep built between 1220 and 1240 with walls two and a half metres thick, and the Burgundian tower of more than 40 metres, added when bishop David of Burgundy rebuilt the castle in the 15th century.
new.tip: The castle itself is hired out for parties, so you mostly admire it from outside. Combine it with the windmill over the town gate a few minutes away.

new.title: Remember the prisoners of Kamp Amersfoort
new.desc: In the woods on the edge of Amersfoort and Leusden stood the longest running German camp in the occupied Netherlands. Around 47,000 people were held here in the Second World War, most of them sent on to other camps, and it is now a national monument.
new.tip: Take your time and walk the full grounds. It is a sober visit, so plan something quiet afterwards.

new.title: Stroll the park behind Slot Zeist
new.desc: Slot Zeist was built between 1677 and 1686 as a pleasure house for Willem Adriaan van Nassau, designed by Jacobus Roman with interiors by Daniël Marot. The town of Zeist has owned it since 1924, and the grounds behind it were turned into an English landscape park in the 19th century.
new.tip: The park is free to walk. Look at the Broederplein and Zusterplein in front of the house, then follow the long Slotlaan into the centre of Zeist.

new.title: Spend a slow afternoon in Wilhelminapark
new.desc: The green heart of Utrecht East was one of the first parks in the Netherlands to be listed as a national monument. Locals come to walk, run and picnic on the grass, and there is a restaurant in the middle of the park.
new.tip: Bring a blanket on a sunny day, as the lawns fill up after work. The Rietveld Schröderhuis is a short walk away if you want to pair the two.

new.title: Cycle a lap of the Máximapark
new.desc: This large city park is the green centre of Leidsche Rijn, the new part of Utrecht west of the Amsterdam-Rijnkanaal, and lies between that district, De Meern and Vleuten. It was called Leidsche Rijn Park until 2011, when it was renamed for the then princess Máxima.
new.tip: Come by bike from the centre, about half an hour. Parkrestaurant Anafora sits inside the park if you want a break in the green.

new.title: Swim out to the island in the Henschotermeer
new.desc: This forest lake near Woudenberg was a drift sand until the 1890s. Sand digging in the 1930s created the lake, which was deepened and enlarged for swimming in 1972. Beaches ring the water, and two wooden footbridges lead to an island in the middle.
new.tip: It opens daily from 8:30 and the gates close an hour before sunset. You need a ticket for entry or parking, which you can buy online in advance.

new.title: Climb De Kaap above the Kaapse Bossen
new.desc: The Kaapse Bossen near Doorn got their name from a former governor of the Cape Colony, who bought the estate around 1750 because the woods reminded him of the forest behind Table Mountain. On the highest point stands De Kaap, a lookout tower of more than 25 metres built in 2006, with a view over the treetops of the Utrechtse Heuvelrug.
new.tip: Start at Theehuis Helenaheuvel, which is open all year, and walk ten minutes to the tower. The trail markers can be hard to follow, so download the route first.

new.title: Walk the star-shaped ramparts of Naarden
new.desc: Naarden is one of the best preserved fortified towns in Europe, with six bastions, a double ring of walls and a double moat that together form a star. Most of the 17th century defences are free to walk, and the Nederlands Vestingmuseum is housed in the Turfpoort bastion.
new.tip: Do the full loop along the walls at an easy pace. Boat tours around the fortifications are also possible.
